opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to realize is why the earlier languages failed to take over. Lisp and Prolog were wonderful for symbolic AI, but they never had a good story for learning. And when AI shifted to machine learning and deep learning, people moved to Python, not because Python is a great AI language, it isn't, but because that's where the libraries were. PyTorch and TensorFlow are really just tensor libraries bolted onto a general-purpose language. So today we have an odd situation: the field that's supposed to be the future of computing doesn't have a language of its own.

TensorLogic is designed so that adopting it doesn't mean giving up what people already have. The core observation is that a logical rule and a tensor equation, an Einstein summation, are essentially the same thing. A rule in Datalog is a join followed by a projection, and that's exactly what an einsum does. So with one construct, the tensor equation, you can write neural networks, transformers, convolutional nets, and also symbolic reasoning, graphical models, kernel machines, all in the same notation. You don't have to choose between the deep learning world and the symbolic world.

The second reason is that it runs on the infrastructure that already exists. It's tensors all the way down, so it compiles to GPUs and lives in the same ecosystem as PyTorch. Prolog asked you to abandon your hardware, your tools, and your way of thinking. TensorLogic asks you to write what you were already writing, more concisely and more transparently.

The third reason is that the timing is right. Everybody now feels the pain points of current AI: hallucinations, lack of reliability, lack of interpretability, the difficulty of reasoning. In TensorLogic you can reason in embedding space and, by lowering a temperature parameter, approach purely deductive reasoning with no hallucinations, while still learning. That's something people actually need today, not an academic nicety.

And languages tend to take over when a field needs a new foundation. Fortran did it for scientific computing, SQL for databases, and the web gave us JavaScript. AI is the biggest shift in computing we've seen, and it's still running on borrowed tools. I'm not claiming adoption is guaranteed; network effects are powerful and Python has a huge head start. But if you give people something that does everything they do now, more simply, and also does things they can't do now, that's how you overcome inertia.

r001.rationale: It says Python prevailed because of its libraries and ecosystem, notes Python’s huge head start and powerful network effects, and contrasts that with Lisp and Prolog’s limits and the costs of abandoning existing tools.

r002.rationale: It calls AI a major shift and says the field needs a new foundation, but does not argue that AI’s centrality could give an AI-suited language the largest user base.

r003.rationale: It names hallucinations as a current pain point and presents TensorLogic’s path toward deductive reasoning with no hallucinations as something users need.

r004.rationale: It mentions interpretability as a pain point and describes TensorLogic as transparent, but does not clearly connect reduced opacity to rapid adoption.

r005.rationale: It says TensorLogic can express current work more simply and describes PyTorch as tensor libraries bolted onto a general-purpose language, but does not identify PyTorch’s underlying complexity as a reason users would migrate.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key thing to understand is why the earlier languages failed, because TensorLogic is really designed around those failures. Take Prolog, which is probably the most successful of the earlier AI languages. Prolog was elegant, it was based on logic, you could do inference in it, but it was slow, it couldn't handle uncertainty, and it couldn't learn. So every time the field moved toward learning and toward dealing with the real world, where things are noisy and uncertain, Prolog just didn't have anything to offer. And then LISP was the other one, and LISP was wonderful as a general-purpose language, but it didn't really give you AI. It gave you a nice environment to program in, and then you had to build everything yourself.

So what happened is that AI moved on, and the languages didn't move with it. Today the dominant paradigm is deep learning, and the dominant tools are things like PyTorch and TensorFlow, which are not really languages, they're libraries on top of Python. And they're great at what they do, but they have no notion of reasoning, no notion of knowledge, no notion of logic. So people are now trying to graft reasoning onto neural networks after the fact, with chain-of-thought prompting and so on, and it's very brittle.

TensorLogic's starting point is the observation that logical inference and tensor algebra are actually the same thing. A logical rule is a join followed by a projection, and in tensor terms a join is a product and a projection is a sum. So a rule is an Einstein summation. Once you see that, you realize you don't have to choose between logic and neural networks. You can have one language where the primitive operation is this tensor equation, and from it you can write a transformer, you can write a Bayesian network, you can write a Prolog program, you can write a kernel machine. All of them become a few lines in the same formalism.

Now, why does that help with adoption? First, because it doesn't ask people to abandon what they're already doing. Everyone in deep learning already thinks in tensors. You're not telling them, come over to this strange world of logic programming. You're telling them, what you already do is logic, you just didn't know it, and here's how you get the rest of the benefits. Second, it runs on the same hardware. The whole reason deep learning won is GPUs, and TensorLogic compiles straight to tensor operations, so you get the speed for free. Prolog never had that. Third, it learns. The earlier languages were purely symbolic, and once learning became the center of AI, that was fatal. In TensorLogic, learning is just gradient descent on the same tensors that represent your knowledge. And fourth, you get something that neural networks on their own can't give you, which is reliable reasoning. If you set the temperature to zero, you get sound deduction, no hallucinations. If you turn it up, you get analogical reasoning and generalization. So you have a dial between the two, and that's exactly what people are groping for right now.

I'm not naive about this. Adoption is hard, and languages mostly succeed for social reasons, not technical ones. But the earlier AI languages failed because they were fighting the mainstream. TensorLogic is trying to ride it.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier languages were “fighting the mainstream” and that language success is social, but it does not explain that widely used languages’ network effects outweighed Lisp and Prolog’s AI advantages.

r002.rationale: It says TensorLogic can appeal to deep learning users because they already work with tensors, but it does not argue that AI’s centrality could give an AI-suited language the largest user base.

r003.rationale: It presents sound deduction with “no hallucinations” as a benefit users are seeking, linking hallucination reduction to TensorLogic’s appeal.

r004.rationale: The response describes reasoning and knowledge as capabilities, but does not say reducing AI systems’ opacity would motivate adoption.

r005.rationale: It says TensorLogic can express several systems in a few lines and uses familiar tensor operations, but does not compare its ease of use with PyTorch’s underlying complexity or predict migration on that basis.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that you have to meet people where they are. Earlier AI languages often asked you to adopt a whole new way of programming, and then you discovered that the libraries, the tools, and the hardware support were somewhere else. Even if the language was elegant, that was a very high price to pay.

The opportunity with TensorLogic is to bring logical reasoning and tensor computation into the same framework. You want to be able to express something as a rule when that’s the natural way to express it, and learn something from data when that’s the natural way to obtain it. Those shouldn’t require two separate systems that you then have to glue together.

But unification by itself isn’t enough. It has to work with the infrastructure people already use, and it has to give them a concrete advantage on a problem they actually have. Can you build something with less code? Can you incorporate knowledge that would otherwise require a lot of training data? Can you understand and change what the system is doing?

If the answers are yes, then adoption can happen incrementally. You don’t have to persuade everyone to abandon their existing tools. You give them something useful, they try it on one part of a problem, and it grows from there. That’s the path I think could make this different—but it’s something you have to demonstrate, not just promise.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier AI languages required a new programming approach and lacked familiar libraries, tools, and hardware support, but it does not explain that widely used languages’ network effects outweighed Lisp and Prolog’s advantages.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that AI’s current centrality could give an AI-suited language the largest user base.

r003.rationale: It does not mention hallucination as a problem TensorLogic could address.

r004.rationale: It presents understanding and changing a system’s behavior as a possible advantage, but does not argue that reducing opacity could motivate rapid TensorLogic adoption.

r005.rationale: It mentions building with less code and adopting incrementally, but does not compare TensorLogic’s ease of use with the complexity underlying PyTorch or predict migration on that basis.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that TensorLogic doesn’t ask you to abandon what already works. One of the problems with earlier AI languages was that adopting the language often meant adopting a whole separate ecosystem. That’s a very high price to pay, even if the language has some beautiful ideas.

The idea with TensorLogic is to bring neural networks and logical reasoning into the same language, with tensors as the common foundation. So you can start with the kinds of models you already use and introduce logical structure where it helps. You don’t have to make an all-or-nothing commitment to a different way of doing AI.

But elegance alone won’t get it adopted. It has to make something people care about easier to build, easier to understand, or more efficient. If we can demonstrate that advantage while fitting into people’s existing workflows, then I think it has a much better chance.

r001.rationale: The response mentions the adoption cost of a separate ecosystem, but does not compare widely used languages’ network effects with Lisp or Prolog’s advantages.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that AI’s centrality could give an AI-focused language the largest user base.

r003.rationale: Hallucination is not mentioned as a reason to adopt TensorLogic.

r004.rationale: The response says TensorLogic might be easier to understand, but does not connect adoption to reducing AI systems’ opacity or predict rapid adoption.

r005.rationale: It does not compare TensorLogic’s ease of use with PyTorch’s complexity or predict that users would migrate.
